question: Why must healthcare resources always be carefully managed and rationed?

options.A: Governments prefer to spend money on education instead of health
options.B: Patients rarely use the medical services provided to them
options.C: Medical equipment is always too expensive to manufacture
options.D: Resources are limited while human healthcare needs are infinite

explanation: You'll see this a lot in practice: money, beds, and staff are finite, but sick patients always need care. That gap means we have to make smart choices! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h1)

question: How does scarcity directly affect your daily life as a nurse on the ward?

options.A: It forces nurses to prioritize care and manage limited supplies efficiently
options.B: It requires nurses to personally fund ward equipment purchases
options.C: It automatically lowers the quality of medications available in pharmacies
options.D: It prevents hospitals from ever admitting emergency trauma patients

explanation: Spot on! Because time and gloves are never endless, great nurses learn to prioritize and manage what they have to keep every patient safe. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h1)

question: What do we mean by the term 'opportunity cost' in health economics?

options.A: The profit a pharmaceutical company makes on a new vaccine
options.B: The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
options.C: The total amount of money a hospital spends on patient medications
options.D: The discount given to patients who pay for medical care in cash

explanation: Think of opportunity cost as what you sacrifice. When you choose to spend your last Naira on transport instead of snacks, the snack is your opportunity cost! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h2)

question: A clinic buys an expensive new lab machine instead of hiring two community health nurses. What is the opportunity cost here?

options.A: The financial cost of maintaining the new laboratory machine
options.B: The total budget allocated to the hospital for the entire year
options.C: The electricity used to power the laboratory equipment daily
options.D: The services and community health work provided by the two nurses

explanation: Exactly. By picking the machine, the clinic gave up the care those two nurses would have delivered to the community. That's the price of the choice! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why is buying healthcare different from buying regular items like shoes or phones?

options.A: The price of medical care never changes based on economic factors
options.B: Patients can easily treat themselves without professional assistance
options.C: Healthcare items are always distributed by governments for free
options.D: People demand healthcare because they want health, not because it is a source of pleasure

explanation: Nobody wakes up wishing to visit the hospital for fun! We seek care simply to get our health back and function well. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h3)

question: What does 'information asymmetry' mean in the healthcare setting?

options.A: Patients understand treatment options better than hospital administrators
options.B: Medical prices are published openly for everyone in the community to see
options.C: Doctors possess much more medical knowledge than their patients
options.D: Health insurance companies have access to all patient medical records

explanation: It just means an imbalance: the doctor or nurse has years of professional training, while the patient often relies entirely on our guidance to understand what's wrong. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h3)

question: In health economics, what does 'supply' actually refer to?

options.A: The total number of patients waiting to be seen in an emergency department
options.B: The quantity of healthcare goods and services providers are willing and able to offer
options.C: The government budget allocated for public health campaigns each year
options.D: The amount of money patients are willing to pay for prescription drugs

explanation: Supply is simply what hospitals, clinics, and health workers make available for people to use—like hospital beds, drugs, and clinic hours. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which of these would most directly lower the supply of healthcare services in a rural health clinic?

options.A: A shortage of trained nurses and doctors willing to work in the area
options.B: Lower prices charged by local pharmacies for basic antibiotics
options.C: An increase in the number of patients seeking routine health checkups
options.D: Higher patient satisfaction scores reported after clinic visits

explanation: Spot on! If health workers aren't there, the clinic simply cannot provide care, no matter how many patients show up. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h4)

question: What does 'market equilibrium' mean in simple terms?

options.A: Consumers buy everything available without worrying about their budgets
options.B: The quantity demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by producers
options.C: The government sets a fixed price for all goods sold in the country
options.D: Producers make maximum profit by charging the highest possible prices

explanation: Equilibrium is the sweet spot where what buyers want matches exactly what sellers are putting out. Everything balances out! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why does the healthcare market struggle to act like a normal open market?

options.A: Doctors and hospitals never charge money for emergency life-saving procedures
options.B: The supply of doctors always matches the exact number of sick people
options.C: Government regulations, insurance systems, and emergencies constantly interfere with free market forces
options.D: Patients always know the exact cost of their medical treatments before admission

explanation: Healthcare isn't like buying shoes. Emergencies happen without warning, and governments step in because health is a basic human right, not just a commodity. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is an economic 'externality'?

options.A: An effect of a transaction that impacts third parties not directly involved
options.B: An unexpected side effect experienced after taking a new prescription pill
options.C: The tax paid by pharmaceutical companies on imported medical drugs
options.D: The total profit earned by a private hospital from foreign patients

explanation: An externality is a spillover effect. It happens when something you do affects other people around you who didn't take part in the original action. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why do public health campaigns often provide free childhood immunizations?

options.A: Pharmaceutical companies give away extra vaccines to charity for free
options.B: Vaccines create positive externalities by building community herd immunity
options.C: Infectious diseases never spread unless children are in school
options.D: Parents refuse to take their children to private clinics for shots

explanation: Brilliant! When you immunize a child, you don't just protect them—you shield the whole community by stopping the spread of disease. That's a powerful positive externality! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of health economics?

options.A: Maximizing profit margins for pharmaceutical manufacturers
options.B: Eliminating all out-of-pocket expenses for hospital patients
options.C: Allocating scarce medical resources to meet healthcare needs
options.D: Regulating the number of medical schools in the country

explanation: Great job thinking about how hospitals run! Health economics simply looks at how we share limited resources like beds, staff, and money to take care of everyone who needs help. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is healthcare different from buying regular goods at the market?

options.A: Illness is unpredictable and human survival is at stake
options.B: Hospitals never face constraints on equipment or staffing
options.C: Medical services are always provided free of charge by the state
options.D: Patients always know exactly what medical treatment they require

explanation: Spot on! You can plan when to buy shoes, but sickness catches you off guard. Because lives are on the line, healthcare doesn't follow normal business rules. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h1)

question: In economics, what two things must a patient have for true 'demand' to exist?

options.A: Approval from a local health ministry
options.B: Immediate availability of a hospital bed
options.C: Financial ability and willingness to pay
options.D: A written referral from a senior physician

explanation: You've got it! Wanting care isn't enough in the market; you also need the means to pay for it. That's what economists call true demand. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h2)

question: How is healthcare 'need' different from healthcare 'demand'?

options.A: There is no practical difference between need and demand in a well-functioning hospital
options.B: Demand is determined entirely by doctors, while need is controlled by health insurance companies
options.C: Need is a clinical judgment of required care, while demand is based on consumer willingness and ability to pay
options.D: Need only applies to surgical procedures, while demand applies exclusively to prescription drugs

explanation: Exactly! As a nurse, you see what the patient clinically needs. But market demand only happens when they can actually afford and agree to pay for that care. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h2)

question: What usually happens to the demand for routine healthcare when out-of-pocket prices go up?

options.A: Demand increases
options.B: Demand fluctuates randomly every day
options.C: Demand remains completely unchanged
options.D: Demand decreases

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When treatment becomes too expensive, fewer people are able or willing to go for routine check-ups. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h3)

question: If household incomes in a community suddenly increase, what change in healthcare use are we likely to see?

options.A: An increase in the uptake of elective and preventive health services
options.B: A total cessation of visits to traditional local healers
options.C: No alteration in how residents access local health clinics
options.D: A sharp decrease in the number of emergency room admissions

explanation: Spot on! When people have more money in their pockets, they can finally afford wellness checks, vitamins, and elective care before emergencies happen. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h3)

question: What does healthcare 'supply' actually measure?

options.A: The total financial debt accumulated by local community hospitals
options.B: The total number of sick people residing within a specific region
options.C: The exact amount of government funding allocated to public health
options.D: The volume of medical services providers are willing and able to offer

explanation: Correct! Supply is simply all the care, beds, and services that hospitals and nurses are ready to provide at any given time. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why can't hospitals quickly increase their supply of healthcare services during a sudden disease outbreak?

options.A: Government regulations forbid facilities from expanding operating hours
options.B: Healthcare relies on heavily trained personnel and strict accreditation standards
options.C: Hospitals operate with an endless surplus of fully qualified nursing staff
options.D: Medical equipment manufacturers never experience shortages of raw materials

explanation: You know how long nursing school is! You can't just train a nurse or doctor overnight. That's why scaling healthcare takes time. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which of these is a major factor that restricts healthcare supply?

options.A: Excessive amounts of idle medical equipment in storage
options.B: An absolute absence of government regulations in hospitals
options.C: Low costs associated with purchasing new pharmaceuticals
options.D: Shortages of qualified nursing workforce and clinical staff

explanation: Right! Even if a ward has empty beds, a shortage of trained nurses and doctors means the hospital cannot safely take in more patients. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h5)

question: How do advanced medical technologies generally impact healthcare supply?

options.A: They can improve efficiency and expand diagnostic capabilities
options.B: They automatically decrease the number of patients seeking care
options.C: They always reduce the total cost of operating a hospital ward
options.D: They eliminate the need for skilled nursing staff completely

explanation: Spot on! New tech helps hospitals run smoother and test patients faster, boosting what the facility can handle. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h5)

question: What happens when a healthcare market reaches 'equilibrium'?

options.A: Healthcare services become completely free of charge
options.B: The supply of doctors far exceeds patient demand
options.C: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.D: Hospital bed shortages disappear permanently everywhere

explanation: Perfect! Equilibrium just means a sweet balance: the amount of care people want matches what the health system is able to give. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why do we often see long waiting lists in healthcare instead of a quick market balance?

options.A: Prices are often distorted or subsidized, causing demand to outstrip supply
options.B: Doctors refuse to treat patients until their medical conditions worsen
options.C: Patients prefer waiting months for elective procedures to save money
options.D: Hospitals deliberately hide available beds to inflate treatment costs

explanation: You nailed it. When care is heavily subsidized or cheap, everyone rushes in, and soon there are more patients than available beds or staff. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h6)

question: What do we call it when a doctor's expert advice strongly convinces a patient to use more medical services than they might have otherwise?

options.A: Supplier-induced demand
options.B: Third-party payment inflation
options.C: Market equilibrium pricing
options.D: An immunization externality

explanation: Exactly! Because patients trust doctors blindly, the experts can sometimes drive up the demand for their own treatments. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h7)

question: How does health insurance lead to 'moral hazard' in healthcare?

options.A: It reduces the total number of qualified nurses working in public clinics
options.B: It insulates patients from true costs, encouraging higher use of medical services
options.C: It forces doctors to recommend unnecessary surgeries to boost hospital revenue
options.D: It legally prohibits individuals from seeking traditional or herbal remedies

explanation: Right! When someone else (like insurance) is paying the bill, patients might not mind running extra tests or picking up treatments they don't really need. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h7)

question: Your hospital ward gets flooded with sudden admissions, leaving you short-staffed. What is the best way to handle patient safety?

options.A: Cancel all routine documentation and vitals checks for the entire day
options.B: Refuse admission to all incoming patients until the next shift arrives
options.C: Increase out-of-pocket treatment prices to immediately lower patient demand
options.D: Adjust staff assignments and prioritize urgent clinical care needs

explanation: Brilliant clinical thinking! When hands are few, a good nurse reorganizes tasks, focusing heavily on those whose lives are most at risk. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h8)

question: Why is it actually helpful for bedside nurses to understand basic health economics?

options.A: It helps them appreciate the operational challenges of resource allocation and patient flow
options.B: It prevents patients from ever experiencing chronic illnesses in the community
options.C: It allows them to negotiate direct commission fees for prescribing medications
options.D: It removes the need for doctors to write formal treatment orders

explanation: Spot on! Knowing economics helps you understand why management makes certain staffing decisions and how best to manage patient beds on your ward. [learn more](GST322_U1_T2#GST322_U1_T2_h8)

question: In simple terms, what does 'demand' mean when we talk about health services?

options.A: The total amount of care that patients want and can use
options.B: The cost of buying medical equipment from abroad
options.C: The total number of doctors in a government hospital
options.D: The maximum number of beds a health center can hold

explanation: You've got this! Demand simply means the healthcare services people need and are able to access. Think of it as the care patients are asking for and using. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is asking for healthcare different from buying regular everyday goods like shoes or food?

options.A: Patients can easily diagnose and prescribe their own meds
options.B: Healthcare services are always completely free from the government
options.C: Sickness usually happens without warning and patients need professional guidance
options.D: The supply of doctors and nurses is totally unlimited everywhere

explanation: Spot on! You can't really plan when you'll fall ill. Because medical needs come suddenly, patients rely heavily on expert advice rather than just shopping around casually. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which group of people usually needs to visit the hospital or clinic the most?

options.A: Teens living in rural villages
options.B: Teenagers in secondary schools
options.C: Healthy young adults working jobs
options.D: Older adults and young children

explanation: Great thinking! The very young and our elderly grandparents have bodies that are more delicate against infections, so they tend to need healthcare services more frequently. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h2)

question: How does low health awareness usually affect when people go to the hospital?

options.A: It often delays people from seeking care until their sickness gets really bad
options.B: It makes them rush in immediately for minor surgeries
options.C: It forces patients to only use expensive private hospitals
options.D: It stops communities from needing health education entirely

explanation: Exactly. When people don't recognize early signs of illness, they often stay at home or use local herbs, only visiting the clinic when things turn into an emergency. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the most important human resource needed to keep a healthcare system running?

options.A: Modern commercial advertising agencies
options.B: Trained doctors, nurses, and midwives
options.C: Private transport and logistics companies
options.D: International pharmaceutical investors

explanation: Too easy! Skilled clinical staff like nurses and doctors are the heartbeat of any hospital; without them, patient care just cannot happen. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h3)

question: A rural health post keeps running out of basic drugs and has no steady electricity. Which part of health economics is this?

options.A: The age distribution of the community
options.B: The supply of health services
options.C: The cultural beliefs of the patients
options.D: The overall consumer demand curve

explanation: You nailed it! Things like drugs, equipment, and steady power are vital parts of healthcare *supply*. When they are missing, the clinic's ability to provide care drops. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is a major problem with making patients pay cash directly out-of-pocket every time they visit the hospital?

options.A: Hospitals automatically get too much money from foreign donors
options.B: Diseases completely vanish from poor communities
options.C: Patients often delay or avoid getting care because they don't have immediate cash
options.D: The number of nurses in the village instantly doubles

explanation: Spot on. Paying cash right at the counter is a huge barrier for many families, forcing them to stay home and suffer rather than seek help. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h4)

question: How does health insurance make it easier for people to get medical care?

options.A: By making all drugs and lab tests completely free to manufacture
options.B: By making it so hospitals no longer need to hire nurses
options.C: By pooling money together so the cost is shared across a large group of people
options.D: By ensuring that no one with insurance will ever catch a chronic illness

explanation: Brilliant! Insurance works like a cooperative contribution—everyone chips in a little so that when someone falls sick, the heavy bill is easily paid from the shared pool. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h4)

question: In healthcare, what do we mean by 'information asymmetry'?

options.A: Pharmacies hide drug prices from the public
options.B: Government agencies control all hospital budgets
options.C: Patients and doctors share the exact same level of medical knowledge
options.D: Healthcare providers have deep medical training while patients know very little

explanation: You got it! It simply describes the knowledge gap: doctors and nurses spent years studying medicine, while patients usually rely on them to explain what is wrong. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal market problem (imperfection) in healthcare?

options.A: Adverse selection where mostly sick people join insurance plans
options.B: Patients having perfect, expert knowledge of all complex medical treatments
options.C: Information asymmetry between the doctor and the patient
options.D: Moral hazard linked to having full health insurance

explanation: Well done! Patients definitely do *not* have perfect medical knowledge. The reality that patients lack this insider knowledge is actually a major market imperfection! [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why is it helpful for a ward nurse manager to understand patient demand trends?

options.A: To stop patients from ever needing admission records
options.B: To schedule staff properly and ensure coverage during heavy illness seasons
options.C: To step in and perform complex surgeries alone in the theatre
options.D: To set market prices for private pharmaceutical drugs

explanation: Exactly right! Knowing when patient numbers are likely to spike (like during malaria or harmattan seasons) helps nurse managers plan shift rosters so the ward isn't short-staffed. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h6)

question: A nurse manager notices that gloves and syringes are being wasted carelessly on the ward. What nursing responsibility does this touch on?

options.A: Conducting large epidemiological research surveys
options.B: Setting national health insurance laws
options.C: Resource stewardship and controlling costs
options.D: Diagnosing rare genetic disorders

explanation: You're doing great! Resource stewardship simply means taking good care of hospital supplies so there's always enough equipment left to treat patients safely without wasteful spending. [learn more](GST322_U1_T3#GST322_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary driving force for providers in a free market healthcare system?

options.A: State control
options.B: Fixed budgeting
options.C: Equal access
options.D: Financial profit

explanation: In a market-based system, the profit motive encourages private entities to invest, innovate, and compete for patients. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h1)

question: How are medical services primarily distributed in a free market economy?

options.A: Through mandatory government rationing
options.B: Based strictly on geographic lottery
options.C: Based on historical hospital quotas
options.D: Through private enterprise and open competition

explanation: Market economies rely on private businesses competing for consumer dollars to distribute goods and services. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h1)

question: What usually happens to the price of a medical service when demand for it rises significantly?

options.A: The price increases
options.B: The price remains strictly fixed by law
options.C: The price drops to zero
options.D: The price becomes irrelevant

explanation: Higher demand for a limited service naturally drives prices upward in a free market environment. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h2)

question: A patient having an emergency heart attack goes to the nearest hospital without comparing prices. Why does this situation break normal market rules?

options.A: Urgent medical needs eliminate the ability to shop around
options.B: Hospitals are legally required to match competitor rates
options.C: Governments strictly ban price tags in emergency rooms
options.D: Emergency care is always free of charge

explanation: True market dynamics require consumers to compare options, which is impossible during life-threatening medical emergencies. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h2)

question: What does information asymmetry mean in the context of healthcare?

options.A: All treatment prices are publicly displayed online
options.B: Patients have equal access to medical textbooks
options.C: Providers know much more about medicine than patients
options.D: Governments hide medical research from the public

explanation: Information asymmetry describes the unequal knowledge gap between trained health professionals and everyday consumers. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why does severe information asymmetry complicate consumer choice in healthcare?

options.A: Insurance companies forbid patients from choosing doctors
options.B: Patients cannot easily judge the quality or necessity of recommended treatments
options.C: Medical prices change every single hour of the day
options.D: Hospitals refuse to let patients read their own paper charts

explanation: Without specialized knowledge, consumers struggle to evaluate whether a proposed medical service is truly necessary or fairly priced. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is a major barrier to price transparency in many healthcare markets?

options.A: Patients are legally barred from asking about expenses
options.B: Hospitals update their price lists every minute
options.C: Final costs are often hidden or unknown until after treatment
options.D: All medical treatments cost the exact same amount globally

explanation: Opaque billing and complex negotiations make it very difficult for patients to know service costs upfront. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h4)

question: How does healthy competition ideally affect providers in a free market?

options.A: It forces them to close their doors within a month
options.B: It encourages them to improve quality and manage costs
options.C: It eliminates the need for any nursing staff
options.D: It prevents them from purchasing new technology

explanation: Competition motivates businesses to attract consumers by offering better value, service quality, and efficiency. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common consequence of relying solely on a free market for healthcare?

options.A: Universal and equal access for all citizens regardless of wealth
options.B: Neglect of unprofitable public health services
options.C: Lack of basic care for uninsured populations
options.D: Geographic concentration of hospitals in wealthy urban areas

explanation: A pure free market distributes care based on ability to pay, which naturally creates disparities rather than universal equal access. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why do private healthcare facilities tend to avoid opening branches in poor rural communities?

options.A: Governments forbid private clinics in rural zones
options.B: The expected financial return is too low
options.C: Rural residents never experience health problems
options.D: Staff refuse to live outside major cities

explanation: Profit-driven enterprises invest where patients have the financial means to pay for services, leading to rural medical deserts. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h5)

question: How can market-driven hospital policies directly impact bedside nursing practice?

options.A: By prioritizing fast patient turnover and tight staffing ratios
options.B: By eliminating all administrative paperwork duties
options.C: By ensuring nurses control hospital budgets
options.D: By guaranteeing unlimited time for patient education

explanation: Corporate models focus on efficiency and cost reduction, which often translates to leaner staffing and faster discharges. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h6)

question: A nurse notices that cost-cutting measures are compromising patient safety on the ward. What is the most appropriate professional response?

options.A: Advocate for the patient and report safety concerns through proper channels
options.B: Reduce nursing assessments to match the hospital budget
options.C: Ignore the issue since hospitals must always maximize profits
options.D: Charge patients directly for extra supplies at the bedside

explanation: Nurses hold a professional duty of patient advocacy, ensuring that business pressures do not compromise safe, ethical care. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why do nurses need to understand health care costs?

options.A: To diagnose complex financial diseases in the community
options.B: To calculate daily profits for the hospital pharmacy
options.C: To help patients navigate financial strain and advocate for them
options.D: To replace hospital accountants during budget reviews

explanation: You will often see how money worries affect your patients. Knowing about healthcare costs helps you support and speak up for them when they face tough financial choices. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h1)

question: What might patients do when health care costs become too high?

options.A: Patients usually demand extra diagnostic tests
options.B: Patients become less likely to ask questions about treatment
options.C: Patients may delay seeking care or skip needed medications
options.D: Patients tend to exercise more to stay out of the hospital

explanation: When medical bills get overwhelming, many people unfortunately try to save money by avoiding the clinic or cutting down their medication doses. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of a direct medical cost?

options.A: Lodging for family members
options.B: Hospital parking fees
options.C: Prescription medications
options.D: Bus fare to clinic visits

explanation: Prescription drugs are directly tied to treating the patient's illness, making them a direct medical cost. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the main difference between direct medical costs and direct non-medical costs?

options.A: Medical costs involve clinical treatment, while non-medical costs involve support services like transport
options.B: Medical costs are optional, while non-medical costs are mandatory for survival
options.C: Medical costs occur in the hospital, while non-medical costs occur at home
options.D: Medical costs are paid by the government, while non-medical costs are paid in cash

explanation: Direct medical costs pay for actual clinical care, while direct non-medical costs cover practical expenses like getting to and from the hospital. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h2)

question: What do indirect health care costs mainly refer to?

options.A: Lost economic productivity and wages due to illness
options.B: The cost of ambulance fuel during emergency transport
options.C: Utility bills and building maintenance for the clinic
options.D: The price of surgical equipment bought by the facility

explanation: Indirect costs are about the money and work time lost when sickness keeps someone away from their job. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h3)

question: A family member stops going to work to care for a sick relative. What type of cost is this?

options.A: Direct medical cost
options.B: Fixed facility cost
options.C: Intangible cost
options.D: Indirect cost

explanation: When a caregiver misses work to help a patient, the lost income is counted as an indirect cost. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is the best example of an intangible cost in health care?

options.A: Hospital room rental fees
options.B: Pain and emotional suffering
options.C: Cost of surgical instruments
options.D: Lost wages from missing work

explanation: Intangible costs are the emotional and physical toll of sickness, like pain, stress, and worry. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why are intangible costs hard to track in a standard budget?

options.A: They cannot be easily measured with a monetary price
options.B: They only happen after the patient leaves the hospital
options.C: They are fully covered by standard health insurance policies
options.D: They are completely preventable with proper hand hygiene

explanation: You cannot easily put a price tag on human pain and emotional stress, so hospital budgets struggle to measure them. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is a fixed cost in a health care facility?

options.A: An expense that increases every time a new patient is admitted
options.B: Wages paid to temporary agency nurses working extra shifts
options.C: An expense that does not change when patient volume changes
options.D: The price of consumable medical supplies like syringes

explanation: Fixed costs, like building rent, stay exactly the same whether the ward is completely full or nearly empty. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which hospital expense usually goes up as more patients are admitted?

options.A: Annual administrative software licenses
options.B: Facility property insurance premiums
options.C: Monthly building mortgage payments
options.D: Disposable syringes and IV tubing

explanation: Medical supplies are variable costs. More patients mean you use more supplies, so the total price goes up. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is a capital cost in health care?

options.A: The cost of disposable bandages used during morning wound care
options.B: A daily expense paid for water, electricity, and cleaning supplies
options.C: The wages paid to housekeeping and security personnel each week
options.D: An investment in long-term assets like buildings or MRI machines

explanation: Capital costs are major, expensive investments used to build facilities and buy heavy equipment that lasts for years. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h6)

question: How do operational expenses differ from capital expenses?

options.A: Operational expenses are optional, while capital expenses are legally required
options.B: Operational expenses are paid only once a decade, while capital expenses are paid daily
options.C: Operational expenses cover daily running costs, while capital expenses cover long-term major assets
options.D: Operational expenses involve patient care items, while capital expenses involve office furniture only

explanation: Operational costs keep the hospital running day by day, while capital costs are for big, long-lasting investments. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h6)

question: How can bedside nurses help lower overall health care costs?

options.A: By preventing hospital-acquired complications and minimizing supply waste
options.B: By charging patients directly for bedside nursing procedures
options.C: By eliminating all diagnostic tests from patient care plans
options.D: By shortening physician consultation times during emergencies

explanation: Stopping problems like pressure sores or infections keeps patients safe, out of intensive care, and saves money on wasted supplies. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h7)

question: A patient is worried about affording their discharge medications. What should you do?

options.A: Pay for the patient's prescriptions using the nurse's personal funds
options.B: Connect the patient with a social worker or financial counselor
options.C: Ignore the financial concern and focus only on physical healing
options.D: Tell the patient to stop taking all medications immediately

explanation: You can help by linking the patient to hospital support staff, like social workers, who can find ways to make their care affordable. [learn more](GST322_U2_T1#GST322_U2_T1_h7)

question: What exactly is an element of cost in healthcare finance?

options.A: The price charged to a patient for bed space
options.B: A penalty fee paid for late supply deliveries
options.C: The total profit made by a hospital ward
options.D: A way to categorize and break down expenses

explanation: Think of cost elements as simple buckets or categories we use to group and track money spent on things like staff salaries and ward materials. You've got this! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it useful for nurse managers to understand basic cost elements?

options.A: To diagnose complex patient illnesses faster
options.B: To calculate individual doctor salaries
options.C: To track spending and justify unit budgets
options.D: To negotiate lower pharmaceutical taxes

explanation: When nurse leaders know where money goes, they can manage their wards better and defend why their unit needs certain resources. Great leadership skill to pick up early! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h1)

question: How would you describe a direct cost in patient care?

options.A: An unexpected emergency expense covered by insurance
options.B: The overall electricity bill for the entire hospital building
options.C: An expense easily traced to a specific patient or unit
options.D: A hidden fee charged by hospital administrators

explanation: Direct costs point straight to one specific place or person—like the exact medication or supplies given to a particular patient. Simple and clear! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is a direct cost for a patient admitted to the surgical ward?

options.A: The general lighting bill for the hospital parking lot
options.B: The monthly salary of the hospital accountant
options.C: The specific surgical gloves worn during their operation
options.D: The cost of repairing the main hospital elevator

explanation: Because those gloves were used directly for that single patient's surgery, they count as a direct cost. Makes total sense when you picture it in the theater! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the main thing that defines an indirect cost?

options.A: It cannot be easily traced to a single patient
options.B: It changes every time a new patient arrives
options.C: It is completely optional for running a clinic
options.D: It only occurs during night shift operations

explanation: Indirect costs are general expenses that keep the whole hospital running rather than belonging to just one patient's bill. [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of these expenses is considered an indirect cost in a hospital?

options.A: Electricity used to light the entire hospital building
options.B: Bandages applied to a specific wound on a patient
options.C: The specific medication prescribed for hypertension
options.D: Surgical instruments sterilized for one specific operation

explanation: General electricity benefits everyone in the hospital, so you can't assign it to just one patient chart. That's why it's indirect! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h3)

question: What happens to fixed costs when patient numbers go up in the hospital?

options.A: They stay exactly the same
options.B: They become direct costs
options.C: They increase significantly
options.D: They drop down to zero

explanation: Fixed costs (like building rent) don't care how many patients walk through the door; they stay stubborn and unchanging regardless! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h4)

question: A sudden malaria outbreak brings a flood of new patients to the ward. Which expense will go up as a result?

options.A: Fixed costs like the monthly rent for the hospital building
options.B: Fixed costs like the long-term equipment lease payments
options.C: Fixed costs like the baseline administrative software license
options.D: Variable costs like disposable syringes and malaria test kits

explanation: More patients mean you need more test kits and syringes! These items change (vary) directly with patient volume. [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is the main feature of a capital cost?

options.A: It involves a large investment in long-term assets
options.B: It changes every time a single patient is admitted
options.C: It covers minor daily items like cleaning supplies
options.D: It must be paid in cash at the end of every shift

explanation: Capital costs are big-ticket investments—like buying a new building or heavy machinery—that stay with the hospital for years. [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which of these is an operational expense (OpEx) rather than a capital investment?

options.A: Purchasing a brand-new MRI scanner for the hospital
options.B: Building a completely new wing for pediatric care
options.C: Acquiring a fleet of new ambulances for emergency services
options.D: Daily cleaning supplies used on the ward

explanation: Cleaning supplies are routine, day-to-day items needed to keep the ward running smoothly, making them operational expenses. [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h5)

question: In healthcare finance, what does 'opportunity cost' mean?

options.A: The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
options.B: The total cost of operating a hospital for one calendar year
options.C: The penalty fee charged for mismanaged nursing budgets
options.D: The financial profit made from treating emergency patients

explanation: Opportunity cost is simply what you have to give up when you choose option A over option B. Every choice has a trade-off! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h6)

question: A clinic spends its limited budget on new vaccines instead of fixing a leaking roof. What is the opportunity cost here?

options.A: The total financial value of the newly purchased vaccines
options.B: The electricity used to power the vaccine storage refrigerator
options.C: The salary paid to the clinic manager for making the choice
options.D: The protection and comfort lost from delaying the roof repair

explanation: Since they chose vaccines, the opportunity cost is the benefit they missed out on by leaving the roof unfixed for now. [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h6)

question: How can a nurse manager use variable costs to plan staff schedules better?

options.A: By eliminating all fixed costs from the hospital accounting ledger
options.B: By anticipating supply needs and staffing levels based on patient admission trends
options.C: By ensuring that building rent decreases during slow hospital months
options.D: By stopping all purchases of direct patient care equipment

explanation: Knowing how costs and patient numbers move together helps you prepare enough hands on deck and supplies for busy seasons! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which action by a nurse manager shows great stewardship of unit resources?

options.A: Ordering excess supplies just to make sure the budget is fully spent
options.B: Monitoring supply usage closely to prevent waste and expired stock
options.C: Refusing to participate in hospital financial planning meetings
options.D: Ignoring indirect costs because they cannot be traced to a single patient

explanation: Keeping an eye on inventory prevents waste and ensures your ward always has what it needs without throwing money away. You're thinking like a true nurse leader! [learn more](GST322_U2_T2#GST322_U2_T2_h7)

question: In old hospital billing systems, where were nursing care charges usually hidden?

options.A: Pharmacy surcharges
options.B: Laboratory diagnostic fees
options.C: Room and board fees
options.D: Direct surgical costs

explanation: Back in the day, hospitals didn't bill separately for nursing care. Instead, they just lumped the cost right into general room and board charges! [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why do modern nurses need to understand a bit of health economics?

options.A: To calculate daily patient medication dosages
options.B: To purchase personal medical equipment
options.C: To prove the financial value of professional care
options.D: To manage hospital pharmacy inventories

explanation: Knowing a bit of economics helps you stand up for your ward, justify why you need more hands on deck, and show management how vital nursing really is. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h1)

question: What usually takes up the biggest chunk of a hospital's daily budget?

options.A: Kitchen provisions
options.B: Building maintenance
options.C: Nursing labor
options.D: Office supplies

explanation: Nurses form the largest workforce in almost every hospital, which means paying nursing staff makes up the largest slice of the operational budget. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h2)

question: What happens when a hospital fails to accurately calculate the cost of its nursing services?

options.A: Patients receive too many medications
options.B: It struggles to set fair prices and manage budgets
options.C: Doctors refuse to admit new patients
options.D: The hospital building loses structural value

explanation: If you don't know what your services actually cost, it's impossible to set fair prices or keep the hospital financially healthy. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which of these is a clear example of a 'direct cost' in nursing?

options.A: Salary of the chief executive officer
options.B: Depreciation of the hospital building
options.C: Wages of the bedside nurse providing patient care
options.D: Monthly electricity bill for the entire hospital

explanation: Direct costs are expenses you can pin directly to a specific patient, like the actual hands-on nursing time spent caring for them. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why are hospital utility bills counted as 'indirect costs'?

options.A: They are shared across the facility and cannot be tied to one patient
options.B: They are paid directly by the nursing department
options.C: They only apply to private hospital rooms
options.D: They change every single day based on the weather

explanation: Things like electricity and water keep the whole hospital running for everyone, so you can't assign them to just one single patient's bill. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the main feature of a fixed cost in a hospital?

options.A: It changes directly with the number of admissions
options.B: It is always paid using foreign currency
options.C: It remains the same regardless of patient volume
options.D: It only applies to surgical ward supplies

explanation: Fixed costs stay steady month after month, whether your ward is completely empty or packed to the brim with admissions. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h4)

question: If a ward suddenly admits many new patients and uses up way more syringes and IV fluids, how are these supplies classed?

options.A: Capital costs
options.B: Variable costs
options.C: Indirect costs
options.D: Fixed costs

explanation: These are variable costs because they go up or down depending on how many patients you currently have on the ward. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the big downside of using a simple flat daily rate (per diem) to cost nursing care?

options.A: it is illegal to use in modern public hospitals
options.B: It ignores individual patient needs and care complexity
options.C: It only calculates the cost of surgical procedures
options.D: It requires complex computer software for every shift

explanation: A flat daily rate assumes every single patient costs the same to nurse, which isn't fair because a critical patient needs way more work than someone resting comfortably. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h5)

question: How does time-driven activity-based costing make hospital budgeting better?

options.A: By calculating costs strictly at the end of each fiscal year
options.B: By measuring the exact time spent on specific clinical activities
options.C: By ignoring staff salaries and focusing only on medical equipment
options.D: By assuming all hospital stays cost the exact same amount

explanation: This method looks at how many minutes tasks actually take, giving a super accurate picture of what care really costs. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the main goal of a Patient Classification System?

options.A: To calculate annual facility building taxes
options.B: To categorize patients based on their nursing care needs
options.C: To track hospital utility and electricity usage
options.D: To determine which doctors are on emergency call

explanation: It sorts patients by how sick they are (acuity) so hospitals can figure out how much nursing time is truly required. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h6)

question: You want to prove your ICU needs more staff than a general ward. Which tool is best to use?

options.A: Patient dietary satisfaction surveys
options.B: Monthly facility utility bills
options.C: General hospital depreciation schedules
options.D: Patient classification system workload data

explanation: Workload data gives you the hard proof of how intense the care demands are in high-acuity areas like the ICU. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a major headache for tracking nursing costs in many Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: Excessive use of automated digital billing
options.B: Reliance on manual record-keeping systems
options.C: Universal health insurance coverage for all citizens
options.D: Complete elimination of out-of-pocket purchases

explanation: When everything is on paper, it becomes very difficult to quickly track exact nursing hours and supplies used. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h7)

question: How do out-of-pocket purchases by patients for basic ward supplies affect hospital records?

options.A: They distort standard cost calculations because items are bought outside the system
options.B: They guarantee that all indirect costs are fully covered by the government
options.C: They make hospital accounting completely automatic and error-free
options.D: They eliminate the need for patient classification systems

explanation: When patients run out to buy their own routine supplies, the hospital's official records miss the true picture of what delivering care actually costs. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is an important job for nurse managers who deal with financial data?

options.A: Approving pharmaceutical manufacturing licenses
options.B: Fixing broken hospital electrical wiring
options.C: Defending staffing levels and resource needs
options.D: Auditing national tax collection records

explanation: Having good cost data lets nurse managers confidently fight for enough staff and supplies to keep patients safe. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h8)

question: What usually happens when nurse managers are left out of hospital financial planning?

options.A: Nursing salaries will increase without administrative review
options.B: Units may suffer from underfunding and increased staff burnout
options.C: Patients will experience faster recovery times on the wards
options.D: Hospitals will automatically receive higher government grants

explanation: If nursing leaders don't have a seat at the financial table, budgets get made without realizing how short-staffed and overworked the wards will be. [learn more](GST322_U2_T3#GST322_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a health care budget?

options.A: To eliminate all unexpected hospital expenses permanently
options.B: To calculate exact salaries for individual doctors and nurses
options.C: To plan and control financial resources for medical services
options.D: To set the retail prices of medications in the pharmacy

explanation: A health care budget serves as a financial plan to guide how money is spent on patient care services. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is financial resource management considered a key part of nursing practice?

options.A: Nurses are solely responsible for auditing hospital accounts
options.B: Nurse managers must directly purchase hospital real estate
options.C: Ensuring supplies do not run out is vital for safe patient care
options.D: Clinical care is completely separate from financial planning

explanation: Proper budgeting prevents critical shortages of daily medical supplies needed at the bedside. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h1)

question: What does equity in a healthcare budget mean?

options.A: Distributing health services fairly so vulnerable populations receive care
options.B: Giving every single department the exact same amount of cash
options.C: Allowing only wealthy patients to access specialized treatments
options.D: Ensuring the hospital makes a profit on every patient admitted

explanation: Budgetary equity focuses on fair distribution so that those in need, including vulnerable groups, can access care. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h2)

question: What does accountability mean for a nurse unit manager regarding finances?

options.A: Personally paying for any broken equipment on the ward
options.B: Deciding how much profit the entire hospital should make
options.C: Setting the tax rates that fund the local health facility
options.D: Being responsible for staying within the assigned departmental budget

explanation: Accountability means managers must answer for how funds are spent in their unit and keep expenses within limits. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which type of budget is used to purchase expensive, long-term equipment like a new MRI machine?

options.A: Capital budget
options.B: Cash flow budget
options.C: Operating budget
options.D: Personnel budget

explanation: Capital budgets are specifically set aside for large, long-term investments and major equipment. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h3)

question: A nurse manager needs to buy daily supplies of syringes and gauze. Under which budget category do these routine expenses fall?

options.A: Investment budget
options.B: Operating budget
options.C: Capital budget
options.D: Construction budget

explanation: Routine, day-to-day operational costs like medical supplies and staff salaries are managed through the operating budget. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is zero-based budgeting?

options.A: Cutting all nursing salaries down to zero during a financial crisis
options.B: Simply adding five percent to whatever was spent last year
options.C: Requiring departments to justify all expenses from scratch every year
options.D: Operating the hospital with zero money until donations arrive

explanation: Zero-based budgeting forces managers to prove the value of every single cost rather than just copying the previous year. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the main drawback of traditional incremental budgeting?

options.A: It requires every single nurse to have a degree in accounting
options.B: It completely stops all purchases of new hospital equipment
options.C: It can carry forward wasteful spending from past years without question
options.D: It takes too much time to calculate compared to zero-based budgeting

explanation: Because incremental budgeting just adds to old totals, past inefficiencies often get repeated automatically. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h4)

question: What does cost containment mean in healthcare?

options.A: Firing all senior nurses to replace them with students
options.B: Closing down hospital wards to save money on electricity
options.C: Reducing expenses without harming the quality of patient care
options.D: Refusing to treat patients who cannot pay cash immediately

explanation: Cost containment is about finding smart ways to save money while keeping patient outcomes safe and high quality. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h5)

question: A hospital ward has very low patient admission numbers for the week. What is a smart cost-containment action the nurse manager can take?

options.A: Turn off the emergency generators to save on diesel fuel costs
options.B: Throw away all leftover medications to clear out the pharmacy
options.C: Adjust shift schedules to avoid paying unnecessary overtime wages
options.D: Refuse to admit any new patients until the following month

explanation: Matching staff levels to patient workload prevents unnecessary spending on overtime during quiet periods. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is an unfavorable budget variance?

options.A: When department managers refuse to write a new financial plan
options.B: When actual expenses exceed the planned budget amount
options.C: When the hospital makes more money than it originally expected
options.D: When staff members refuse to work overtime shifts

explanation: An unfavorable variance means the facility or unit spent more money than it was allocated. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why must nurse managers review monthly financial reports?

options.A: To catch and investigate budget variances before they become major deficits
options.B: To determine which nurses should be disciplined for making mistakes
options.C: To change the medical diagnoses written in patient clinical charts
options.D: To calculate the annual bonus for the hospital's chief executive officer

explanation: Monthly reviews allow managers to spot overspending early and take corrective action. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary way many Nigerian patients currently pay for healthcare services?

options.A: Full government sponsorship
options.B: Free community charity funds
options.C: Out-of-pocket spending
options.D: Private international grants

explanation: A large portion of healthcare financing in Nigeria relies on direct out-of-pocket payments by individuals. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical challenge faced in Nigerian healthcare budgeting?

options.A: Inflation driving up the cost of imported medical drugs
options.B: Delays in the official release of approved budget allocations
options.C: Instantaneous release of excess government funds every single week
options.D: Unpredictable revenue caused by low health insurance coverage

explanation: Delayed funding releases are a known challenge, so instantaneous weekly funding is incorrect. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of doing an economic check on health care services?

options.A: Reducing the salaries of clinical nursing staff
options.B: Comparing costs and health outcomes of different programs
options.C: Eliminating all out-of-pocket spending for patients
options.D: Maximizing the number of hospital beds in a region

explanation: Economic appraisal looks at alternative treatments by weighing what they cost against their clinical results to help guide funding choices. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why do health managers need to use economic appraisals?

options.A: Private hospitals operate without any financial limitations
options.B: Healthcare resources are limited relative to community needs
options.C: Government budgets for health care never experience constraints
options.D: Clinical outcomes are identical across all treatment modalities

explanation: Because funds, staff, and supplies are always limited, health systems must choose which interventions give the best value for care. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h1)

question: If a patient pays transport fare to reach the clinic, what kind of cost is this?

options.A: Intangible psychological cost
options.B: Direct medical expense
options.C: Indirect productivity cost
options.D: Direct non-medical cost

explanation: Travel expenses are direct money costs caused by illness, but the money is not paid directly to the hospital or medical staff. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h2)

question: What are lost wages called when a patient misses work due to being hospitalized?

options.A: Direct medical costs
options.B: Indirect costs
options.C: Direct non-medical costs
options.D: Capital overhead costs

explanation: When people cannot work because of illness, the lost productivity is measured as an indirect cost in health economics. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h2)

question: When is it best to use a cost-minimization analysis?

options.A: When one intervention has far superior clinical effectiveness
options.B: When comparing programs with completely different goals
options.C: When health outcomes cannot be measured numerically
options.D: When competing interventions produce identical health outcomes

explanation: Cost-minimization is used when two options give the exact same health results, so the choice comes down to which one is cheaper. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h3)

question: A clinic checks two different brands of the same blood pressure drug that work equally well and are equally safe. Which analysis should they use?

options.A: Cost-minimization analysis
options.B: Cost-benefit analysis
options.C: Cost-utility analysis
options.D: Cost-consequence analysis

explanation: Since the drugs have the same safety and effectiveness, the study only needs to find the least expensive option. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h3)

question: How are health results usually measured in a cost-effectiveness analysis?

options.A: Natural physical units like life-years gained
options.B: Monetary amounts in local currency
options.C: Patient satisfaction survey scores
options.D: Quality-adjusted life years exclusively

explanation: Cost-effectiveness uses real health measures like blood pressure lowered, lives saved, or extra years of life. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h4)

question: What does the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) actually measure?

options.A: Extra cost required to achieve an extra unit of health outcome
options.B: Total hospital expenditure divided by total annual admissions
options.C: Difference between nurse salaries and drug procurement costs
options.D: Net monetary benefit minus patient out-of-pocket expenses

explanation: The ICER compares how much extra money a new treatment costs against how much extra health benefit it gives. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h4)

question: What does QALY stand for in health economics?

options.A: Quantified Access to Local Youth
options.B: Quality-Adjusted Life Year
options.C: Quick Assessment of Living Years
options.D: Qualified Allied Labor Yield

explanation: QALY stands for Quality-Adjusted Life Year, which is a standard way to measure both the length and quality of life gained from a treatment. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why do health policy makers like using cost-utility analysis?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need to calculate financial costs of nursing care
options.B: It avoids assigning numerical values to patient quality of life
options.C: It measures clinical success exclusively through laboratory blood test values
options.D: It allows comparison of completely different types of health interventions using a common unit

explanation: Using QALYs lets health planners compare completely different programs, like mental health care versus surgical services, on the same scale. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h5)

question: What makes cost-benefit analysis different from other types of economic studies?

options.A: Outcomes are measured strictly as physical life years gained
options.B: Both costs and health outcomes are expressed in monetary terms
options.C: It ignores indirect productivity losses completely
options.D: It focuses solely on hospital administrative expenditures

explanation: Cost-benefit analysis turns health outcomes into money values so that the benefits and costs can be directly compared in currency. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is a major ethical worry about using cost-benefit analysis in health care?

options.A: Requiring complex computer software for simple arithmetic
options.B: Placing a financial monetary value on human life and health
options.C: Failing to account for nurse staffing shortages in wards
options.D: Measuring outcomes in natural units instead of currency

explanation: Many people and healthcare workers feel uncomfortable putting a direct price tag on human life and suffering. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a limitation of health economic appraisals?

options.A: Potential neglect of vulnerable or hard-to-reach populations
options.B: Guaranteed elimination of all hospital financial deficits
options.C: Reliance on assumptions that may not fit local settings
options.D: Difficulty in accurately quantifying all indirect costs

explanation: Economic studies help guide decisions and find efficient practices, but they do not automatically wipe out a hospital's money problems. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h7)

question: How can nurse managers use findings from economic appraisals in their daily work?

options.A: To replace clinical judgment with rigid financial spreadsheets
options.B: To eliminate the need for patient consent in clinical research
options.C: To determine individual nurse disciplinary actions and salary cuts
options.D: To provide evidence when advocating for cost-effective staffing and equipment

explanation: Managers can use economic data to support requests for better ward supplies and staffing without lowering the quality of care. [learn more](GST322_U2_T5#GST322_U2_T5_h7)

question: What do macroeconomic indicators provide for a country?

options.A: A numerical snapshot of economic health
options.B: A count of registered nurses
options.C: Individual patient health records
options.D: Hospital room occupancy rates

explanation: Macroeconomic indicators give a broad numerical summary of how a nation's economy is performing overall. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to understand basic economic trends?

options.A: Economic trends directly affect hospital funding and resources
options.B: Nurses must calculate national tax allocations
options.C: Clinical diagnoses depend on inflation rates
options.D: Hospital management requires nurses to trade stocks

explanation: Great question! National economic performance dictates government budgets, which trickle down to hospital supplies, staffing, and facility maintenance. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the main rule for deciding if economic activity counts toward a country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP)?

options.A: It must be performed exclusively by citizens
options.B: It must be funded by the federal government
options.C: It must happen within the physical borders of the country
options.D: It must involve imported medical supplies

explanation: Think of GDP like a fence around the country. Everything produced inside those physical borders counts, no matter who owns the business! [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which of these activities counts toward Nigeria's GDP?

options.A: A Nigerian nurse working in a London hospital
options.B: A retired Nigerian citizen receiving a pension abroad
options.C: A foreign company manufacturing drugs entirely overseas
options.D: A foreign doctor treating patients at a private clinic in Lagos

explanation: You've got this! Because the medical service takes place physically inside Nigeria, it contributes to Nigeria's GDP. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main rule for deciding what counts toward a country's Gross National Product (GNP)?

options.A: Approval by the World Health Organization
options.B: Physical location inside the national borders
options.C: Tax exemption status of the business
options.D: Citizenship or ownership by permanent residents

explanation: While GDP looks at geography, GNP focuses on who owns the production or who performs the work based on citizenship. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h3)

question: How does GNP treat profits earned by a foreign-owned company operating inside Nigeria?

options.A: They are added directly to Nigeria's GNP
options.B: They are converted into government bonds
options.C: They are doubled in Nigeria's GNP
options.D: They are excluded from Nigeria's GNP

explanation: Remember, GNP only counts output generated by citizens and permanent residents, so foreign-owned production inside the country is left out. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the main difference between GDP and GNP?

options.A: GDP is calculated monthly while GNP is calculated every decade
options.B: GDP includes inflation while GNP excludes all taxes
options.C: GDP measures health services while GNP measures manufactured goods
options.D: GDP uses geographic location while GNP uses ownership and citizenship

explanation: The core distinction is simple: GDP cares about where production happens, while GNP cares about who owns the production. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why might a developing country have a GDP that is higher than its GNP?

options.A: The government spends more money on imported medical equipment
options.B: Citizens are working fewer hours in local clinics
options.C: Inflation rates are lower than neighboring countries
options.D: Foreign companies own a large share of domestic production and send profits abroad

explanation: When foreign firms generate massive output inside a country, it boosts local GDP, but those profits leave the country, keeping GNP lower. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h4)

question: How do governments use healthcare spending as a percentage of GDP?

options.A: To calculate individual patient prescription costs
options.B: To set the daily working hours for hospital staff
options.C: To determine the required passing grade for nursing students
options.D: To measure how much national wealth goes toward medical care

explanation: This ratio shows the proportion of a country's total economic output dedicated to keeping people healthy and running health services. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h5)

question: What does a growing GDP fail to guarantee regarding a national health system?

options.A: That nurses will receive higher salaries
options.B: That the country will stop importing medications
options.C: That the wealth will automatically translate into better healthcare access
options.D: That hospitals will have electricity every day

explanation: Economic growth provides potential revenue, but political will and budget priorities dictate whether that money actually reaches clinics and patients. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT measured by GDP or GNP?

options.A: Total market value of goods
options.B: Total income generated by businesses
options.C: Overall population health and happiness
options.D: Monetary value of services rendered

explanation: GDP and GNP only measure money and production. They don't capture human well-being, happiness, or social health directly. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why can an increase in pollution sometimes cause GDP to rise?

options.A: Factories become more efficient at cleaning the air
options.B: Governments fine hospitals for environmental damage
options.C: Citizens spend less money on protective face masks
options.D: More people require medical treatment for respiratory illnesses

explanation: It's a paradox! Environmental damage that makes people sick actually increases economic activity because citizens spend money on doctor visits and drugs, which boosts GDP. [learn more](GST322_U3_T1#GST322_U3_T1_h6)

question: What does Gross National Product (GNP) measure?

options.A: The total amount of physical cash printed by the central bank
options.B: Only the money earned by foreign companies inside the country
options.C: The total cost of running public hospitals for one year
options.D: The total economic value produced by a country's citizens globally

explanation: Think of GNP as tracking the wealth created by a country's people, no matter where in the world they are working! You've got this. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why does a country's GNP matter for nursing and healthcare?

options.A: It directly dictates the daily shift schedules of clinical nurses
options.B: It determines the overall economic capacity available to fund public health and facilities
options.C: It sets the national passing score for professional nursing board exams
options.D: It measures the exact number of patients admitted to emergency wards

explanation: A wealthier nation (higher GNP) generally has more funds to build hospitals, buy equipment, and support healthcare workers. Makes total sense, right? [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h1)

question: What does a high amount of out-of-pocket health spending usually tell us about a country?

options.A: A weak public financial safety net for citizens
options.B: An exceptionally strong and free healthcare system
options.C: That citizens pay very low taxes overall
options.D: That the government is meeting all international health targets

explanation: When patients have to pay cash for almost everything at the hospital, it usually means the government's safety net isn't quite covering them yet. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why do economists look at health spending as a percentage of GNP rather than just raw cash amounts?

options.A: It stops inflation from happening in local community pharmacies
options.B: It calculates the exact salary every registered nurse should earn
options.C: It allows fair comparison between countries with different economic sizes and populations
options.D: It predicts the exact number of disease outbreaks in a year

explanation: Using percentages helps us fairly compare health spending between big economies and smaller nations without getting confused by different currency values. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h2)

question: Under the Abuja Declaration, what percentage of their annual budget should African governments put toward health?

options.A: Five percent of private sector corporate profits
options.B: Ten percent of all international donor funds received
options.C: Exactly 50 percent of the total Gross Domestic Product
options.D: At least 15 percent of the annual national budget

explanation: The famous Abuja Declaration set a benchmark of at least 15% for national health budgets. Great to keep in mind for your exams! [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h3)

question: A clinic nurse notices frequent shortages of basic drugs and sutures. What is a major reason for this in many African nations?

options.A: International agencies ban the importation of basic surgical items
options.B: Nurses generally mismanage the medical supplies in hospital warehouses
options.C: Patients refuse to accept free medications from the government
options.D: National health budgets frequently fall short of the Abuja Declaration target

explanation: When budgets fall short of targets like the Abuja 15%, clinics struggle to buy everyday essentials like gloves, drugs, and suture materials. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h3)

question: How has Nigeria's federal budget allocation for health traditionally compared to the Abuja target?

options.A: It matches the exact international average for wealthy nations
options.B: It has consistently hovered well below the 15 percent benchmark
options.C: It has consistently exceeded 25 percent of the national budget
options.D: It is funded entirely through private corporate sponsorships

explanation: Sadly, Nigeria's health allocations have historically stayed in the single digits, well below that 15% goal. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why does spending most of a health budget on recurrent costs (like salaries) hurt long-term care?

options.A: It stops international donors from sending vaccines to the country
options.B: It forces hospitals to close down outpatient departments permanently
options.C: It leaves very little money for capital investments like equipment and infrastructure
options.D: It prevents clinical nurses from receiving their monthly salaries on time

explanation: If all the money goes straight to paying overhead and salaries, there's little left over to buy new machines, build wards, or upgrade facilities. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h4)

question: What usually happens when a country struggles to collect enough domestic taxes for public services?

options.A: A sudden surplus of funds for hospital construction
options.B: Complete elimination of out-of-pocket patient fees
options.C: Immediate achievement of the Abuja Declaration target
options.D: Increased reliance on external grants and borrowing

explanation: When local tax revenue is low, governments often have to seek loans or donor grants to keep funding public sectors like healthcare. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h5)

question: Why does high national debt servicing negatively affect public health budgets?

options.A: It directly increases the number of patients seeking private insurance
options.B: It forces international health organizations to withdraw all nursing staff
options.C: It automatically lowers the market price of essential pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: It drains government revenue that could otherwise be allocated to social sectors like health

explanation: When a huge chunk of national income goes to paying off debts, less money is left in the purse for hospitals, schools, and health programs. [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is a common clinical consequence for nurses when the health sector is chronically underfunded?

options.A: Higher salaries and improved workplace safety standards
options.B: An abundance of modern diagnostic equipment on every ward
options.C: Decreased patient wait times in accident and emergency units
options.D: Severe burnout from heavy patient-to-staff ratios

explanation: Underfunding means fewer staff and fewer resources, leaving the nurses on duty to handle overwhelming patient crowds. Burnout is a very real challenge here! [learn more](GST322_U3_T2#GST322_U3_T2_h6)

question: A patient with severe malaria arrives late at a clinic because they couldn't afford transport or consultation fees. What economic factor is mainly to blame?

options.A: Excessive government spending on preventative health education
options.B: Too many nurses working in rural primary health centers
options.C: High reliance on out-of-pocket health expenditure
